title: burststep phased probe — scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal log for an exploratory micro-benchmark I ran to characterize short-duration "burststeps" — repeated, phased microbursts separated by small quiescent windows — and their interaction with our scheduler, batching, and kv-cache warmup. Not a polished report; notes to self + raw numbers for later triage.

Setup summary:
- Model: pythia-6b-ish equivalent (float16), baseline compiled kernels with auto-quant path disabled.
- Host: single A100-40GB instance; 8 logical worker threads in harness.
- Runtime build: local branch `burststep-scheduler-v2` (see GH ref).
- Harness: custom harness around wrk2-style generator, capable of scheduling phased bursts (js runner).
- Input: short prompts (~30 tokens), total generation target ~64 tokens.
- Arrival pattern: 5-phase cycle repeated 100x = 500 bursts total. Phase timings (ms): 
    phase A: 0ms (instantaneous spike), 50 requests in 80ms
    phase B: quiet 200ms
    phase C: ramp 0->40qps over 120ms (smooth)
    phase D: quiet 150ms
    phase E: microburst 30 reqs over 60ms
- Batching: dynamic batching enabled, max_batch=64, batch_timeout_ms=8, continuous batching ON.
- KV cache: cold for first 5 cycles, then warmed by repeating many similar prompts.

Key commands (harness snippets):
- `python harness.py --pattern burststep --cycles 100 --burst-config bursts.yaml --workers 8`
- `nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 10` (coarse GPU utilization)
- pprof traces grabbed for 3 representative cycles (early cold, mid warm, late warm).

Raw metrics (aggregated windows, representative numbers):
- First 5 cycles (cache cold): avg QPS observed during spike windows ~410 qps (very bursty), p50 latency 42ms, p95 220ms, p99 760ms. GPU util low-ish (47%) during cold because of serialize+warm penalty.
- Mid run (after warmup ~cycle 20): spike window avg QPS 620 qps, p50 18ms, p95 112ms, p99 320ms. GPU util ~78%.
- Late run (stabilized cycles 80-100): spike window avg QPS 580 qps, p50 20ms, p95 98ms, p99 290ms. Observed slight oscillation in queue length during phase C ramps.
- Quiet windows: 0–4 qps, tail still shows elevated p99 from earlier backlog for ~30ms after spikes.

Notable observations / anomalies:
1) Batching inertia: when phase A (instant spike) fires, workers create many small batches in first 40ms due to low batch_timeout_ms. This causes high token amortization overhead and elevated p95. When I increased batch_timeout to 12ms, p95 improved by ~18% at cost of p50 +6ms in quiet ramps.

2) KV-cache priming cost: first few requests post-cold showed ~1.8x decode latency due to kv allocation and page-fault-like overhead in runtime. Warmup by synthetic repeated prompts brought this down after ~12 similar requests. Consider prefill API or a light-weight prefix-caching priming pass for dedicated pools.

3) Scheduler backpressure during phased ramps: when phase C ramps toward higher qps, the scheduler sometimes splits requests across two worker pools (hot vs normal) causing out-of-order batching and a small spike in p99 (~50–80ms). Hypothesis: our routing policy sees transient overload and mis-classifies compatibility buckets.

4) Eviction / small-gc events: on one run I saw GPU mem trim (CUDA reported page migrations) at cycle ~37 — coincided with an unrelated housekeeping daemon started by infra. Need to ensure test nodes are isolated when doing these quick-cycle microbenchmarks.

Representative ASCII throughput trace (time axis ~ms, coarse):
[cycle sample, time 0..800ms]
0   |█████████████████-----       spike A (80ms) ~410qps
80  |-----                    quiet B (200ms)
280 |███────███────███         ramp C (120ms) 0->40qps
400 |-----                    quiet D (150ms)
550 |██████--                  microburst E (60ms) ~240qps

Quick conclusions / actionable follow-ups:
- Increase batch_timeout_ms to 10–12ms for this workload family; improves p95 during instantaneous spikes with acceptable p50 tradeoff.
- Prototype a tiny prefill/priming endpoint that sends 2 warmup requests per new sequence to mitigate kv cold penalties for dedicated customers with short prompts.
- Add a small routing hysteresis: don't immediately move traffic between pools on sub-500ms overload signals; require 2 consecutive overload ticks. This should reduce the out-of-order batching seen in ramps.
- When running microbench cycles, pin out cloud housekeeping and disable dynamic host autoscaling to get reproducible traces.

Open questions / experiments to run next:
- Re-run with quantized model variant (4-bit) to see whether batching inertia still dominates or GPU becomes the limiter.
- Measure effect of increasing max_batch from 64 -> 128 with same timeout to see cost/latency tradeoff under phase A spikes.
- Try changing worker-thread count (8 -> 12) to see if more concurrency reduces microburst tails or just increases contention.

Notes to self:
- Save pprof dumps + harness logs under GH artifact link (GH:repo/inference-harness#842) and annotate with cycle ids.
- Share these quick notes with Rhea/Timo, schedule 30m sync to decide which mitigation to try first (hysteresis vs timeout tweak vs priming).

End of scratchpad (raw) — keep as intermediate working doc.
